The feeder identifier acts as a quasi-identifier that narrows down a specific geographic area served by the electrical grid. In the context of the ontology, this relates to Location and Identifying data. Combined with other fields (date, consumption patterns), it could enable re-identification of specific consumers within a small service area (70 housing units). Under GDPR Article 4(1), data that can be used to identify a natural person directly or indirectly is personal data. The feeder number, while an infrastructure identifier, serves as a geographic locator that reduces the population to a small, identifiable group.

The substation identifier, like the feeder, is a quasi-identifier that pinpoints a specific geographic region. In the ontology context, this maps to Location and Geographic data. When combined with the feeder number, it further narrows the geographic scope, increasing re-identification risk. Under data minimization principles (GDPR Article 5(1)(c)), if the substation number is not strictly necessary for the data processing purpose, it should be anonymized or pseudonymized to prevent linkage to specific consumer groups.

The date field is a standard temporal identifier. While it can serve as a quasi-identifier when combined with other data (e.g., specific consumption spikes on particular dates), on its own it does not identify an individual. In the ontology context, it does not map to any specific personal data class. The temporal granularity (daily) is sufficient to prevent identification of specific individuals. Standard data protection practice does not require anonymization of date fields in aggregate infrastructure datasets.

This is an aggregate count of housing units (70 in the sample). In the ontology context, it does not directly map to IndividualProfile or any personal data class. The count is already de-identified by nature. However, if the count were very small (e.g., 1-5), the risk would increase significantly.
